title: Groundwater Audit
question: Did arsenic and nitrate decline at repeatedly sampled wells in San Bernardino County, 2000 to 2023, and where does an LLM help or quietly err in answering?
one_liner: A checked reference analysis of public USGS groundwater chemistry paired with bounded, scored model runs on frozen tasks under two prompting conditions.
aim: Determine whether dissolved arsenic and nitrate declined at repeatedly sampled wells in San Bernardino County between 2000–2011 and 2012–2023, and test whether a language model, with and without a structured analytical workflow, reproduces a checked reference analysis of the same data.
hypothesis: Pooled period comparisons will reflect changes in which wells were sampled rather than change at wells; only a consistent cohort can answer the question. A structured workflow with validators will reduce model errors relative to a neutral prompt.
conclusion: No decline in nitrate at cohort wells. Arsenic is slightly lower on average, by an amount within replicate precision and coincident with a laboratory change and a drop in reporting limit. The model produced correct numbers under both conditions. The structured workflow raised cost without reducing errors; residual errors were definitional and required reading answers against reference definitions.

summary.question: Did arsenic and nitrate go down at the same wells over two decades, and can an AI analyst be trusted to answer that correctly?
techniques: Frozen analysis tasks with mechanical scoring
summary.result: No decline in nitrate. Arsenic is slightly lower, by less than measurement noise, alongside a laboratory change. The AI analyst got the numbers right under both prompting styles; its only errors were in definitions, caught by reading rather than by checking counts.

pitfalls.text: Of the wells in the arsenic record, {{arsenic.pooled_vs_cohort.wells_only_early}} were sampled only early and {{arsenic.pooled_vs_cohort.wells_only_late}} only late; the pooled medians compare different wells
The arsenic reporting limit fell from {{arsenic.limits_by_year.0.max}} to {{arsenic.limits_by_year.-1.median}} µg/L as the laboratory changed; substituting half the limit would manufacture a decline
Every nitrate sample appeared twice, as N and as NO3; pooling without reconciling doubles the count
Two model runs volunteered cohort analyses on the same wells that pointed opposite ways because of unstated weighting

finding: The pooled nitrate median fell from {{nitrate_as_n.pooled_vs_cohort.pooled_early.km_median:.2f}} to {{nitrate_as_n.pooled_vs_cohort.pooled_late.km_median:.2f}} mg/L as N and the pooled arsenic median rose from {{arsenic.pooled_vs_cohort.pooled_early.km_median:.1f}} to {{arsenic.pooled_vs_cohort.pooled_late.km_median:.1f}} µg/L between 2000 to 2011 and 2012 to 2023. Neither is a change at wells. The late period sampled different wells, and only a minority of wells appear in both periods.

At the {{nitrate_as_n.paired_change.n_pairs}} nitrate wells sampled in both periods, {{nitrate_as_n.paired_change.decline}} declined and {{nitrate_as_n.paired_change.increase}} increased. At the {{arsenic.paired_change.n_pairs}} arsenic cohort wells, {{arsenic.paired_change.decline}} declined and {{arsenic.paired_change.increase}} increased with {{arsenic.paired_change.indeterminate}} indeterminate because of non-detects; the sign test gives p = {{arsenic.paired_change.sign_test.p_two_sided:.3f}}, but the median within-well ratio of {{arsenic.paired_change.wilcoxon_both_detected.median_ratio_late_over_early:.3f}} is a small measured shift inside replicate precision and coincident with a laboratory and reporting-limit change.

The evaluation ran {{evaluation.runs}} model sessions on frozen tasks under neutral and structured-workflow prompts, scored mechanically and then read against a rubric. The structured workflow cost {{evaluation.workflow_cost_uplift_pct:.0f}} percent more and did not reduce errors; definitional failures were caught by reading answers against reference definitions, not row counts. Published original grades remain the baseline.

The separate corrected schema scorer re-evaluated the same recorded answers without new model calls: {{v2.passed}} of {{v2.checks}} mechanical checks passed, versus {{evaluation.passed}} of {{evaluation.checks}} under original scoring, with {{v2.major}} major and {{v2.critical}} critical failures. Artifact review corrected a false-negative composition keyword match in the first schema version. Wording and scientific correctness still require rubric review.

traps.how: Pooled period medians moved in opposite directions for the two constituents, and neither reflected change at wells; the consistent cohort told a different story.
Arsenic reporting limits dropped sharply across the record; non-detects were treated as intervals and the median estimated by Kaplan-Meier, never substituted.
Every nitrate sample appeared twice, as N and as NO3, and nitrate-plus-nitrite was stored under its own name; pooling without reconciling definitions doubles the count.

Two model runs volunteered unrequested cohort analyses on the same wells that pointed in opposite directions because of unstated weighting; both numbers reproduce and neither run said why they differ.

figures.caption: Period medians for all samples, one per well, and the consistent cohort. The pooled bars move; the cohort bars barely do.
Same well, early period against late period. Nitrate scatters around the diagonal; arsenic leans slightly below it.
Reporting limits of non-detects over time by laboratory. The arsenic limit drops an order of magnitude when the laboratory changes.
Sampling coverage by year. Effort is uneven and the late period is thin.

not_claimed: No remediation effect, aquifer-wide improvement or health conclusion.
No human time saved; no analyst session was timed.
Two repetitions per cell are not evidence of broad superiority of either prompting condition.
